newsitem.title: UK: Cobalt drifts, other minor metals slow.
newsitem.headline: Cobalt drifts, other minor metals slow.

text.p: Trading in the industrial minor metals remained sluggish over the past week as the approaching Lunar New Year in China and other parts of the Far East helped to slow trading activity.
Price remained at little changed levels, though cobalt, despite the continuing chaos in Zaire, drifted back.
On Thursday an official of Zaire's state run mining company Gecamines said he saw no immediate danger from a rebel advance.
This confirmed talk from informed trade sources which has recently circulated in Europe.
Currently traders believe Zaire produces about 5,000 tonnes of cobalt per year of which 1,000 tonnes is of high grade quality.
Although the rebels have advanced into the rich mineral bearing region of Shaba they still remain around 400 miles away from Lubumbashi, the hub of the cobalt and copper belt.
Others said that cobalt production was below 5,000 tonnes.
"Even if production is running at around 5,000 tonnes it is still fairly low which may be another reason why the market has not seen a strong mark up in prices," one trader said.
Production from Gecamines has fallen at a steady rate over the last decade.
According to the Cobalt Development Institute annual production in 1995 was 4,146 well down on the dizzy heights reached in 1986 of over 14,000 tonnes.
But even if prices continue to drift several traders said the market will find support from a booming aerospace industry.
Cobalt ingots held steady but there was talk of some Russian offers.
Iridium against the backdrop of further Japanese demand, firmed. Traders said iridium had the potential to climb to $250 an ounce as the metal is being increasingly used in catalytic converters.
Rhodium after recent intense downside pressure showed signs of levelling off but several traders believed the market would soon resume its downside trend against the backdrop of oversupply.
Gallium held firm, while vanadium was also stable at higher levels. Traders said both metals continued to experience nearby supply problems.
